The question of whether humans are fundamentally good or evil is one of the most enduring debates in philosophy and psychology, with genuinely opposing viewpoints and research outcomes. [d1] reports that Yale University experiments with babies suggest "even the youngest humans have a sense of right and wrong, and, furthermore, an instinct to prefer good over evil," offering empirical support for innate goodness. [d4] similarly presents Mencius's philosophical argument that "human nature is good" because humans inherently possess tendencies toward benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, and propriety. [d5] and [d6] summarize historian Rutger Bregman's position that "people are fundamentally good," with humans having evolved to be compassionate and cooperative, and that war and violence arose from civilization rather than from nature. [d7] nuances this view, arguing that humans are "fundamentally good? Yes, for the most part," but acknowledges that "some bad apples" exist and that even good people can do terrible things due to groupthink or misinformation. On the opposing side, [d3] contends that "people are only good as so far it's good for them to be good" and that "civilization is only skin deep," pointing to widespread violence and suffering as evidence against fundamental goodness. [d2] captures the philosophical divide most clearly, presenting Rousseau's claim that "man was naturally good" and corrupted by society alongside the classical liberal view that "there is something stubborn in man that refuses to bend," illustrating that no single answer commands consensus across traditions or research.
